questions.prompt: Which unit-circle explanation shows why sin(-x) = -sin x?
questions.prompt_markup: Which unit-circle explanation shows why sin(-x) = -sin x?

choices.text: The points for x and -x are (a, b) and (-a, b), reflections of each other over the y-axis, so their sines are opposites.
sin(-π/6) = -1/2 = -sin(π/6), so the rule always holds.
The points for x and -x are (a, b) and (a, -b), reflections over the x-axis, so the sines b and -b are opposites.
A negative sign can always be moved outside a function, so sin(-x) = -sin x.

questions.correct_answer: The points for x and -x are (a, b) and (a, -b), reflections over the x-axis, so the sines b and -b are opposites.
questions.grading_note: Equal arcs in opposite directions from (1, 0) give points that mirror over the x-axis. The others name the wrong reflection, use a false general rule (cos(-x) = cos x, not -cos x), or check one value.

questions.prompt: Which unit-circle explanation shows why cos(x + 2π) = cos x?
questions.prompt_markup: Which unit-circle explanation shows why cos(x + 2π) = cos x?

choices.text: Adding 2π moves the point to the opposite side of the unit circle, and opposite points on the circle have the same x-coordinate, so the cosine is the same.
cos(x + 2π) = cos x + cos 2π = cos x + 1.
Adding 2π travels one full turn around the unit circle and ends at the same point, so the x-coordinate (the cosine) is the same.
cos(0 + 2π) = 1 = cos 0, so the rule always holds.

questions.correct_answer: Adding 2π travels one full turn around the unit circle and ends at the same point, so the x-coordinate (the cosine) is the same.
questions.grading_note: The circumference is 2π, so x and x + 2π give the same point. The others distribute cosine over a sum, describe the wrong motion, or check one value.

questions.prompt: Which unit-circle explanation shows why tan(x + π) = tan x?
questions.prompt_markup: Which unit-circle explanation shows why tan(x + π) = tan x?

choices.text: Adding π gives the point (a, -b), a reflection over the x-axis, so tan(x + π) = -b/a = -tan x, which is not tan x.
Adding π gives the opposite point (-a, -b) of (a, b), and tan = (-b)/(-a) = b/a, the same ratio.
Adding π travels a full turn, so the point is the same.
tan(π/4 + π) = 1 = tan(π/4), so the rule always holds.

questions.correct_answer: Adding π gives the opposite point (-a, -b) of (a, b), and tan = (-b)/(-a) = b/a, the same ratio.
questions.grading_note: Half a turn takes (a, b) to (-a, -b); both coordinates change sign, so the ratio is unchanged. The others use the wrong point, mistake π for a full turn, or check one value.

questions.prompt: Is f(x) = sin x cos x even, odd, or neither?
questions.prompt_markup: Is f(x) = sin x cos x even, odd, or neither?

choices.text: Even: a product of two functions is always even
Odd: f(-x) = sin(-x)cos(-x) = (-sin x)(cos x) = -f(x)

questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: How does periodicity prevent sin x from having an inverse on all real numbers?
questions.prompt_markup: How does periodicity prevent sin x from having an inverse on all real numbers?

choices.text: Each value appears only once in every period, so periodicity changes nothing.
Periodicity makes sin increasing everywhere, so it has no turning points.
Each value repeats every 2π, so an output does not determine its input.
Periodic functions are undefined at multiples of 2π, which breaks the domain.

questions.correct_answer: Each value repeats every 2π, so an output does not determine its input.
questions.grading_note: Not one-to-one. The others are false: values repeat, sin is not increasing everywhere, and it is defined at multiples of 2π.

questions.prompt: Why is arcsin(-1/2) = -arcsin(1/2)?
questions.prompt_markup: Why is arcsin(-1/2) = -arcsin(1/2)?

choices.text: arcsin(-1/2) = 7π/6 because sin(7π/6) = -1/2, which is -arcsin(1/2).
sin is even on [-π/2, π/2], so sin(-π/6) = 1/2, giving arcsin(-1/2) = π/6.
A minus sign can always be moved outside any function, so arcsin(-a) = -arcsin(a).
sin is odd on [-π/2, π/2], so sin(-π/6) = -1/2, giving arcsin(-1/2) = -π/6 = -arcsin(1/2).

questions.correct_answer: sin is odd on [-π/2, π/2], so sin(-π/6) = -1/2, giving arcsin(-1/2) = -π/6 = -arcsin(1/2).
questions.grading_note: Oddness on the restricted domain carries over to the inverse. The others use an output outside [-π/2, π/2], call sin even, or use a false rule about moving a minus sign.
